The Outline of the Essential Meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* (Concluded).
Composed by the Tiantai Bhikṣu Lingyao.
I. General Title.

In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, "Prajñā" (Wisdom) is the mind shared by both ordinary beings and sages. That it remains unmanifest for ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle is due to four [factors].
This is because when one is defiled by the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), one is unable to give rise to the great function of the vajra.

Now, if one penetrates these with the vajra, the wisdom-observation of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-prajñā*) will manifest before one; it will not only destroy the four abidings (*catvāra āśrayāḥ*) of the six ordinary realms.
Furthermore, this dispels the doubts and attachments of those of the Two Vehicles. Generally, the first half of the volume clarifies dwelling in, descending into, and departing from signs;

all states that are "neither this nor that" are included therein. The *pāramitās* are the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna gate; fundamentally, there is no distinction between self and other, nor between reaching and not reaching.
This is simply because ordinary beings are entirely deluded and the Two Vehicles are attached, such that neither has yet opened the secret treasury nor seen it.

The "Jewel Island" (Ratnadvīpa) refers simply to arriving there. This applies to everything from the latter half of the volume onward that clarifies the equality of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
This is because the general encompasses the particular, and the particular is distinct from the general;

though the general and the particular are two, that which they signify is but one. Therefore, it is impossible to separate them from the general title and provide a distinct explanation. Moreover, this...

The purport of the Sautrāntika school lies solely in dispelling doubts and harmonizing with the Dharma. This is not only evident in the specific passages, but even in this general title, the great meaning is clear:
"Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā" signifies the Great Emptiness that sweeps away all marks; "Samatāpāramitā" signifies the harmonization of all things as Mahāyāna.
The general and the specific illuminate one another like a string of pearls held within a shell. If one were to speak of them as three aspects...
Furthermore, the Secret Treasury (Guhyakośa) is divided into general and specific categories, with its meaning opening into five layers as commonly elucidated; these shall not be enumerated here.
△ Second, the specific text has three parts. First, the introductory section (nidāna-parivarta) has two parts. One, the general introduction (sāmānya-nidāna).
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
△ Second, the specific introduction:
At that time, the World-Honored One, at the hour of eating, put on his robes and took up his alms bowl, entering the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.

Having completed his sequential begging within the city, he returned to his original location. When he had finished his meal, he set aside his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and spread out his seat.
And sat down.

To reveal the Tathāgata’s complete embodiment, great function, and ultimate profound wisdom, he used the mundane, ordinary, and shallow matters of daily life—food and clothing—as a means to initiate this teaching.
This is just as the *Lotus Sūtra* opens with its introductory chapter, or as the *Contemplation Sūtra* does.

The meaning of "suffering as the sequence to bliss" cannot be explained by taking it as a symbolic expression of the Dharma—such as the patience of cessation (*śānti-kṣānti*) or the foremost emptiness (*parama-śūnyatā*).
Nor should it be taught as using the precepts as the foundation for meditative concentration and wisdom.
For if one treats this as an extraordinary discourse on the laws and regulations, one immediately loses the meaning of the sequence as it pertains to ordinary practical application.

△ Second, the main body of the treatise has two parts: first, explaining the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* by way of the characteristics of abiding, descending, and departing after the arousal of the bodhicitta;
second, detailing the absence of any dharma prior to abiding and descending in order to manifest the *Prajñāpāramitā*.

Now, the essential purport of the Prajñāpāramitā section lies in using the water of emptiness-wisdom to universally wash away clinging attachments. It brings together all eighty-one categories as Mahāyāna.
The first half of the volume clarifies the methods for abiding, subduing, cultivating, and entering; it emphasizes washing away attachments and eliminating the dust of delusion.
Therefore, it frequently explains that "all things are not [what they appear]," thereby manifesting the great function of the Vajra, while simultaneously providing a convenient means for realization.

Because it enters into the true reality (*tathatā*) of ultimate emptiness, although there are such explanations as "names" and so forth, they primarily refute the direct [teachings] while harmonizing with the peripheral ones;

in general judgment, this belongs to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. In the latter half of the scroll, Subhūti has already understood how to dwell in the state of transcending and detaching from signs.
When names and meanings are cast aside, one looks back to the original cause; yet even at the very beginning, there remains the dharma of "arousing the aspiration" (bodhicitta).
As long as ignorance has not been removed, the source remains turbid; the secret treasury is difficult to open, and the stages and abodes are difficult to enter.
Although there may be merit from cultivation, it is feared that traces of form still remain. Thus, one cannot avoid failing to abide well in abiding, and failing to subdue well in subduing. And so...
Since cause and effect, as well as cultivation and realization, would all fail to be ultimately equal, there is a further inquiry. To this, the Tathāgata directly reveals:
"Within the realm of True Suchness (tathatā), the provisional names of 'sentient beings' and 'Buddhas' are extinguished; within the wisdom of equality, the forms of 'self' and 'other' do not exist.
If there were even a single dharma of 'arousing the mind' to be attained, it would [be a deviation] upon the very substance of equality."

There is increase and decrease; one must know that the *prajñā* of the true mark (*dharmatā*) is profoundly still and eternally abiding, wherein not even a speck of dust can be established, and where names and marks such as "existence" or "non-existence" can never be found.
If one speaks of "existence," then there is immediately a "non-existence" that stands in opposition to that existence.
This constitutes a dharma of relative increase and decrease; it is not the essence of equality.

Therefore, it is said that there is truly no dharma by which one generates the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. This "truly non-existent dharma" is not only non-existent, but moreover, it is even the absence of non-existence.
Existence and non-existence are both dispelled, and equality is thereby revealed.

Since, at the very outset, one realizes that the nature [of all things] is inherently equal, then from cause to fruit, there is nothing to be attained, nothing to be cultivated, no adornment, and no saving of sentient beings; all these are utterly absent.
They converge in equality. Therefore, although one vigorously cultivates and realizes cause and effect, there is nothing that does not arise from cultivation based on the complete nature;
cultivation is entirely contained within the nature. When nature and cultivation are unified, one enters the ultimate shore of the Mahāyāna.
Generally, in these texts, the meaning of "all dharmas are suchness" is that they are neither real nor unreal—all are the Buddha-dharma. These dharmas are equal; suchness is...
Movement. And all these are called "bases" (*āyatana*). All point toward the other shore of the Mahāyāna gate.
From shallow to deep, first breaking down and later reconciling—such is the nature of the Dharma. Someone may say:

"In the first half of the volume, there are also statements such as 'neither real nor unreal, all are called [names],' and in the second half of the volume, there is also the phrase 'all are neither. How can you claim that the former..."

Is the first half of the scroll solely concerned with the sublation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) in the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, while the second half is solely concerned with the assembly of dharmas (*dharma-samavasaraṇa*) in the *Prajñāpāramitā*?
Answer: There are two points to consider. First, the purports of the preceding and succeeding sections each have their respective secondary and primary emphases.

Second, they manifest the difference between the perfect fusion of essence and function (*tǐ-yòng yuánróng*) and their sequential distinction. This is because, in the first half of the scroll, Subhūti has just—

Although one perceives the Prajñā that is free from marks, if the mind of self-characteristics has not yet been severed, one cannot immediately realize that all dharmas of the holy and the ordinary converge in the reality-mark of equality.
It is therefore appropriate to use the wisdom of true emptiness to universally sweep away all attachments.

For this reason, there is an abundance of statements clarifying "shattering" and "negation," while the discourse on "being thus named" is revealed only intermittently; it is only upon reaching the final conclusion of the meaning that [the ultimate truth is fully disclosed].

In this passage, when the Buddha briefly points toward the principle that there is neither reality nor unreality, it is precisely because the purport of the teachings throughout his entire life lies in the Perfect [Teaching].
If Śāriputra had attained realization of the true mark (*dharmatā*) at this point, the latter half of the fascicle would have been unnecessary.

However, as for the actual capacity of the audience, they were situated only at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties; thus, they could only receive the teaching that "all things are simultaneously shattered" in order to clear away delusions.
Those who cling to their emotions have not yet realized that all things are entirely included within the gateway of the Mahāyāna;

thus, the first half of this fascicle merely clarifies the emptiness of true reality (*śūnyatā*) and the sublation of appearances. Consequently, there arises again the question regarding the methods for entering and abiding in existence.

The Buddha, knowing that the disciples' faculties were gradually becoming clear and expansive, was able to apply the principle of the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) to those who were ready to receive it. Therefore:
Although these words carry the implication that what is "immediately" [perceived] is not real, their meaning actually clarifies the principle of the equality of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

From this point onward, one enters ever deeper; accordingly, one accords with the causes and effects of the three karmas, as well as the eighty-one categories and eighty thousand dharmas of arising and ceasing pertaining to both the mundane and supramundane realms—all of which enter the Mahāyāna of the true mark, yet remain like waves...
The meaning of the *pāramitā* is thus fully revealed. While these two chapters are slightly interconnected in their phrasing, their meanings are actually distinct and categorized;

each has its own primary and secondary aspects and must not be confused. Furthermore, whereas the preceding section consists entirely of words that negate both extremes, the latter preserves the teaching that [reality] is neither like a dream nor an illusion.
This serves to manifest the perfect integration of essence and function, which is not subject to sequential progression.
As for the distinction: although the preceding section refuted attachments to clarify the function of wise contemplation, its intent did not depart from the essence of the true mark (dharmatā);

hence there was the teaching that "names exist, yet they are neither real nor unreal. Although the subsequent section harmonizes all phenomena to reveal the essence of the other shore (pāramitā), its intent does not project outward;
hence there is likewise the statement that "both are neither real nor non-existent. This precisely refutes and reveals the characteristics [of reality].
The essential principle of perfect interfusion is that while essence and function are distinct, they are mutually identical, each being both primary and secondary.
Now, for the first part, there are two sections. First, the praise and inquiry:
At that time, the Elder Subhūti, amidst the great assembly, rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, and placed his right knee [upon the ground].
He descended to the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying: "It is rare, World-Honored One!

The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One, how should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved their mind toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their minds?"

As for Śāriputra’s sudden praise of what is rare and marvelous: it is because the Tathāgata, in his daily conduct, is no different from an ordinary person and does not reveal even a hair’s breadth of sharp edges or protruding corners;
yet, his inner realization of compassion and wisdom transcends the nine realms of existence, and it is for this reason that it is rare and marvelous.
It is that while their conduct is the same as others, their minds differ from others. It is like a woodcutter who is on a mountain and a hermit who is also on a mountain;
they are the same in being on the mountain, yet the reason for being there differs.
As for the Tathāgata, from his appearance in the world until now, it has always been thus. Yet, as for Subhūti, he was unaware of this until today, when he suddenly beheld it.
Jue realized he could no longer restrain himself; his three karmas leaped with joy, and he suddenly praised [the Buddha], saying, "How rare!

By this single praise alone, he became fundamentally different from one who was as if deaf or mute, or one who silently endured rebukes while clearing away filth, or one who wept in sorrow upon stripping off his clothes.
○ Immediately thereafter, he explained the reason for his exclamation of rarity, saying: "The Tathāgata skillfully protects and sustains us."
Regarding the various bodhisattvas: it should be known that from the *Avataṃsaka* until now, the World-Honored One has protected and entrusted them from time to time;
there has never been a time when he did not protect and entrust them. Thus, while one may simply say "protected and entrusted," one cannot say "well-protected and well-entrusted.
This is because such [latter] expressions involve conceptual designations (*vyavahāra*), which provoke agitation; they are partial rather than perfect. Now, however, with...
They shared the same food and clothing, and he rarely displayed any outward signs of his condition; yet, with compassion protecting him from within, he was truly the most intimate of kin.

Thus, he is called "good. This is like the case of the fifth-ranking official Lun, who would rise ten times during the night to inquire after and examine his nephew’s illness, yet upon returning home would lie down and sleep peacefully.
However, when his own son was ill, although he did not rise to inquire or examine him, he remained awake throughout the entire night. Furthermore...
Furthermore, one should know that the "rare and marvelous" is not identical to the "entrustment through protection," yet it does not lie outside of that entrustment;
the "entrustment through protection" is not identical to the "rare and marvelous," yet from the outset it is never separate from the rare and marvelous.

This is like how the "single thread" of the sages of the world is not identical to "loyalty and empathy," yet it does not lie outside of loyalty and empathy; "loyalty and empathy" is not identical to the "single thread," yet from the outset it is never separate from the single thread.
In essence, for the Sage, these are inherently unified and complete; they may simply be called "the One" or "the Rare.

However, for the worthy one, they cannot avoid being differentiated and are thus regarded as "loyalty and reciprocity" (zhong-shu) and entrusted accordingly. As for how a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide and descend [into practice], before Subhūti had yet seen [this truth], he attained...
(Note: The final character "得" indicates the sentence is incomplete, likely leading into a description of Subhūti’s realization.)

"It is enough to have little; one does not aspire to what is excellent. Now that we have caught a glimpse of even a single speck [of the truth], a great resolve has suddenly arisen within us, and we joyfully admire the Supreme Vehicle (Agrayāna).

Therefore, it is said: "We have already given rise to this rare mind. However, after giving rise to this mind, we desire to proceed directly to the stage of being entrusted and protected by the Tathāgata;
yet fearing that such entry may not be sudden, we must necessarily descend from there and apply ourselves to practice.

Now, as for entering by gradual stages, I know that the Tathāgata likewise began his journey from abiding in subduing [the mind], continuing until the present day of skillful protection and entrustment.
Since the Saṃgha has sought the Buddha, they ought to follow the Buddha’s practice; therefore, after asking about the arousal of the bodhicitta, they inquire:
"How should one abide? How should one subdue [the mind]? △ Second, the answer and explanation, which is threefold. First, the granting of approval.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas;
he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. Listen attentively now, and I shall explain it for you.
Sons and daughters of good family who have resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this manner and subdue their minds in this manner."
Regarding that mind, one should know that it is well-guarded and well-entrusted; this is the realization of the Tathāgata’s practice.
Since the realization of Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) and [the Buddha’s] own mind are not distinct, the Buddha bestowed his seal of approval. △ Second, receiving the essential meaning.
"Indeed, World-Honored One, we wish and desire to hear it. △ Third, the actual clarification, which is divided into two parts:
first, clarifying the abiding and descending by examining them through the broad and the concise; second, manifesting the merits by entrusting them to the names and meanings of hearing and retaining.
The first part is further divided into two: first, a brief answer regarding the abiding and descending as being free from marks; second, an extensive explanation of the abiding.
The descent from signs consists of the teaching of Prajñā through two gates—the extensive and the concise—which simultaneously benefit those of sharp and dull faculties.
First, the concise answer to the second [question]; first, the answer to the descent.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way:
'Regarding all categories of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation;
whether with form or without form; whether with perception, without perception, or neither with nor without perception—I shall [liberate them all]..."

He causes them to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and brings them to final liberation. Although he thus liberates immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings, in reality there is no sentient being who attains liberation.
Why is this? Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span, then he is not a bodhisattva.
△ Second, the answer regarding abiding.

"No, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, can the space of the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir be measured?

However, when it comes to seeking the practice of ultimate protection and entrustment, his question—“How should one abide and subdue [the mind]?”—is once again confined to the views of the Hīnayāna.

It was guaranteed that he had not yet been able to receive further advancement, but was merely subject to censure.

Now, however, since Śūnyatā-utpāda (Subhūti) has witnessed this rarity, he has suddenly resolved his mind upon the Great [Vehicle]. He is now capable of expanding his limited emptiness through the Great Emptiness and broadening his limited wisdom through Great Wisdom.

This refers to the time when one should apply [exertion]. That you have hitherto sunk into emptiness, dwelt in quiescence, and clung to a partial truth was itself the realm of the Hīnayāna.
Now that you seek to become a Buddha, you must likewise not remain fixed in a single state;

you should extensively practice the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), for only then will you be truly established. However, while practicing the six perfections, you must not cling to the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
One must establish all dharmas from the root of non-abiding; thus, every practice is a cultivation arising from the perfection of nature, equal to empty space.

This further uses the wondrous practices of the Mahāyāna to encourage and advance Subhūti, effectively entrusting him with wealth and property, leaving it entirely to him to manage, expend, or bestow as he sees fit.

As for the successive examinations through physical forms and the fruits of the Dharma to lead you forward, this is to cause all dharmas to interpenetrate, to exhaust all remaining doubts, and to cause all to enter the gate of the Mahāyāna.

Now, Subhūti is like a swift falcon or hawk that returns to the correct path upon seeing the shadow of a whip; therefore, he answered directly, saying: "Setting forth..."
The mind and its ultimate reality are not two distinct things. Since the cause is already free from characteristics, how could the fruit be a physical phenomenon?
One must understand that at the moment emptiness arises, the diamond-like wisdom has already pierced the cataracts of the four eyes; thus, the realization of formlessness is revealed in its entirety.
Within this, there are three layers of comprehension. First: "One cannot see [the Buddha] by means of physical marks."
Second layer: The bodily marks described by the Tathāgata are themselves not bodily marks. Third layer: If this interpretation were erroneous, the Buddha would have rebuked it;

Is it not the case that they are non-characteristics? You must know that defilement and purity, the holy and the ordinary—all are non-existent.

Furthermore, while you have previously known that the worldly phenomena of the six realms of existence are all false and illusory and have thus abandoned them, how could you have known that even the characteristics of the two vehicles, bodhisattvas, and Buddhas are likewise false and unreal?
This is because their vision was partial; [the teaching] is now opened to lead them toward the perfect.
[The Buddha] fulfills [the aspiration]. He draws forth that small emptiness and returns it to the great emptiness.

Since the Buddha attained enlightenment, he has gradually and skillfully guided others, wishing to open up their small emptiness and small wisdom; however, as their capacities were not yet ready, he remained silent for the time being.
Now, having found the opportunity to open them, which accords with the Buddha’s original intent, he therefore draws it out and elaborates upon it, saying: "Whatever exists..."
All marks are entirely false and illusory. If one perceives that all marks are not marks, then one sees the Tathāgata;

To see [thus] is the *Prajñāpāramitā*. One must know that these words which reveal the reality are based on the Buddha’s intended meaning.

It is perfect; therefore, it is pointed out in various places. Yet, because the capacities and dispositions [of beings] have not yet matured, they only grasp at the efficacy of True Emptiness (śūnyatā) in its power to demolish and disperse [delusions].
One must not, in this regard, cling to the literal text and thereby harm the intended meaning. △ Second, revealing that both the hearing and the meaning are profoundly deep, in two parts:
First, the excellence of the person who hears.

Virtue.

Human beings inherently possess this nature. When it appears to you for the first time, you consider it extraordinary; yet in the Buddha’s perfect illumination, such people have never been lacking.
It is not only during the Buddha’s own lifetime that there are many with the capacity [for awakening].

Even after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, in the final five hundred years—a time when strife and contention are rampant—there are still those who are like blue lotuses blooming amidst fire, who upon hearing this Prajñāpāramitā can give rise to true faith. However, their past...

Having planted roots that are profound and deep, you have been seen and known by the Buddha; you are no ordinary person. A single thought of pure faith is itself the functional application of the vajra.
It sweeps away all myriad thoughts and the dust of emotional afflictions, leaving manifest alone the single thought of the numinous awareness of prajñā.
This is precisely the convergence of the ten thousand dharmas into one. Once you realize this One, then all matters are completed. This is the first thought of the initial mind.
Contemplating Prajñā: Because one’s realization of the profoundly deep Prajñā is equal to that of the Buddha, the Buddha knows all and sees all of this.
△ Second, the depth of the meaning heard.
Why is this? These sentient beings no longer possess the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span.

They have no notion of dharmas, nor do they have any notion of non-dharmas. Why is this? If these sentient beings take up signs with their minds, they immediately become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
If they take up the notion of dharmas, they likewise become attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span. Why?
For this reason, to cling to and grasp at the signs of what is not the Dharma is to cling to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span.
Therefore, one should neither grasp at the Dharma nor grasp at what is not the Dharma. For this purpose, the Tathāgata has constantly said:
"O Bhikṣus, you should understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma."

Once this single thought-moment has been revealed, it is like one who has lost their way and suddenly awakens; they will never again be deluded. Like refined gold once extracted, it is no longer mixed with ore.
All characteristics are utterly detached, and perfect luminosity remains untainted. Therefore, it is said:
"There is no longer the mark of self, the mark of others, the mark of sentient beings, or the mark of a life-span. "No longer" means not again, not once more. How could there be anything else?

Ordinary beings possess the four marks [of conditioned existence]. Furthermore, they lack the realization of the Dharma-marks attained by the noble ones; yet, they do not forget the wisdom of contemplation that perceives the non-existence of dharmas through emptiness.
This is like the *jaṭāmāṃsī* cloth mentioned in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra, which has not yet been removed.

Therefore, it is said: "If one clings to even a single non-dharma, this constitutes the four marks of birth and death. For this reason, one must not cling to either the mark of dharma or the mark of non-dharma. Next, then...
Citing this passage to explain and establish the point, it says: "The Dharma I teach is like a raft for crossing a river spoken to those on this shore.

There is no fixed location. Once the shore has been reached, both [the raft and the desire for it] should be abandoned. Excerpted from the "Raft Simile" chapter of the *Āgama Sūtra*.
△ Second, clarifying through the evidence of the resultant dharma.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?

Or has the Tathāgata preached any dharma? Subhūti replied, “As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata could [attain].”
[The Buddha] said: "Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable and ineffable; they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas.
Why is this so? Because all noble ones and sages are distinguished precisely by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛtadharma*)."

Since the Buddha has already revealed that the essence of *prajñā* is manifest, one is free from both the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristics of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), not merely being free from what should be abandoned when delivering sentient beings.

Fearing that Subhūti had not yet grasped this, the Buddha again cited how the Tathāgata delivers all sentient beings before realizing *bodhi*, and having completed his cultivation, preaches the Dharma for the sake of beings, in order to test him. He said:
"Does the Tathāgata attain bodhi? Is there any teaching? This question contains two intentions:
first, to open the way for profound emptiness to give rise to great wisdom; second, to immediately harmonize all dharmas within the Mahāyāna.

Having reached this point, Śūnyatā-utpāda’s mind was already fully integrated; thus, his verbal response was imbued with this integration and inclusiveness, unlike his previous impulsive remarks. Its...

It is said: "If one discusses how the Tathāgata attained the fruit naturally through cultivation over kalpas, and has since appeared in the world preaching the Dharma everywhere—yet I understand the meaning of the Buddha’s recent raft-parable as being that there is no fixed doctrine, then what is called 'bodhi' is not a fixed dharma;

Deviating and confused, yet falsely claiming it to be "Right Equality" (samyaktva), one addresses those lost in delusion as if they were dreaming, using the provisional name "Perfect Enlightenment.
In reality, within the essence of Prajñā, not even a single birth can be apprehended;

how then could there be a Buddha’s Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi spoken of in contrast to birth? Since even the name has no fixed existence, how could there be any actual attainment? This is what is meant by that which is taught:

The Dharma is like administering medicine according to the illness; since even the "sicknesses" of sentient beings cannot be found, how could there be fixed dharmas such as existence that are taught in relation to emptiness?
Since dharmas have no fixed nature, how can they be spoken of? Fearing that the principle of their lack of fixity may not yet be clear:
Therefore, he explains it again, saying: "If there is anything that can be spoken of, one immediately falls into the four marks.

For this reason, all things are neither graspable nor speakable; this summarizes the aforementioned absence of the four marks. "Not a dharma" summarizes the aforementioned absence of the mark of dharmas.
"Not a non-dharma" summarizes the aforementioned absence of the mark of non-dharmas. This single section concludes the formal response.
I have grasped the purport shown above; yet, fearing that the meaning of "neither being nor non-being" has not yet been fully clarified, I shall explain it further:
If one discusses the wisdom realized through cultivation, there are indeed distinctions of depth and shallowness, or great and small, among the various ranks of sages;
however, as for the *prajñā* (wisdom) that manifests the departure from all marks (*lakṣaṇa*), it is identical in all cases. Do not say, "My wisdom is small and my emptiness is small. Do not...
This is identical to the Great Emptiness Prajñā of the Tathāgata. For if there are the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*), they are not unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).
If one retains the mark of dharmas (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), it is not unconditioned; if one retains the mark of non-dharmas (*adharma-lakṣaṇa*), it is likewise not unconditioned.

While the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* briefly states only that one must be free from the four marks, here, based upon unconditioned Prajñā, we further clarify that there are neither marks of dharmas nor marks of non-dharmas. How could this be...?

This is not an expansion upon the previous section concerning the subduing of the mind and its detachment from marks. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the non-abiding production of the mind according to the nature of merit has three parts:

“Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, “It would be very great, World-Honored One.”
Why is this? Because this merit is not the nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says that the merit is great.

Since the previous brief answer concerning non-abiding in giving had not yet clarified how one gives or how the merit of non-abiding is profound, he again brings forward the aforementioned characteristics of the abundance of merit to serve as a comparison for the function of the nature of non-abiding.

This is the very root [of the Dharma]. It is not the nature of merit; rather, it is giving while attached to signs. As for giving, even if one were to offer the two great chiliocosms filled with the seven treasures, "non-abiding" means not dwelling upon the ten realms of sages or ordinary beings.
Its merit is superior. To reveal in detail the merits of the human realm—how could this not be an expansion of the previous practice of non-abiding giving?
II. Showing how the function of the nature gives rise to the Buddha-dharma.

Furthermore, Subhūti, if there should be someone who, from within this sutra, receives and maintains even as little as a single four-line verse and explains it to others, their merit would surpass that [of the former]. Why is this?
Subhūti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* of all Buddhas—all emerge from this sutra.
To uphold and expound this sutra is to abide in non-abiding *prajñā* while practicing for one’s own benefit and the benefit of others.
The present statement that it "produces the bodhi of all Buddhas" is a brief answer concerning the merit that is as inconceivable as space.
In the subsequent detailed comparison, the specific characteristics of that merit will be fully set forth, along with the person and the location. △ Second, [the section] traversing all...
The Dharma Point on the Non-abiding Mind, Part Two. First, the detailed explanation of non-abiding, in four sections. First, the Buddha-dharma:
"Subhūti, that which is called 'Buddha-dharma' is precisely not Buddha-dharma."
The so-called "two characters" refer to the bodhi of all Buddhas mentioned previously.
The "not [so]" two characters refer to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. △ Second, the four fruits.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have the thought, 'I have attained the fruit of stream-entry'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A stream-enterer is called one who has entered the stream, yet there is nothing entered.
He does not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; thus he is called a stream-enterer. Subhūti, at that time...
"What do you think? Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? A Sakṛdāgāmin is so called because he returns once more; yet in reality, there is no coming or going."
"This is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Anāgāmin have this thought:
'I have attained the fruit of an Anāgāmin'? Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that?
An Anāgāmin is named 'one who does not come back,' yet in reality there is no such thing as 'not coming back. For this reason, he is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think?"
"How is it? Can an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?

World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought, 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would thereby be clinging to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span."
"World-Honored One, the Buddha has declared that I have attained the samādhi of non-contention (*araṇā-samādhi*), being foremost among men; I am a *arhat* who is foremost in being free from desire.
World-Honored One, I do not harbor such a thought as: 'I am an *arhat* free from desire. World-Honored One, if I were to harbor such a thought as:
'I have attained the path of an *arhat*,' then the World-Honored One would not say of me, Subhūti, that I am one who delights in [the dharma]."
Regarding the practitioner of *araṇā* (non-conflict): because Subhūti truly has no practice, he is called "Subhūti who delights in the practice of *araṇā*.

As for "further traversing the four fruits," this refers to the dharmas already cultivated and realized by one born in the four *ārūpya* (formless) realms, which [the interlocutor] then puts forward as questions. To cause...

He himself has invited the state of non-abiding. When Subhūti spoke of "non-existence" for each and every thing, this was precisely the clear testimony that all noble sages are of unconditioned dharmas. △ Third, the Buddha’s attainment.
The Buddha said to Subhūti, "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain any dharma?
No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained no dharma."
"The Buddha had no attainment of dharmas under Dīpaṃkara Buddha. This raises Śākyamuni’s own cultivation and realization to examine the matter;
it differs from the previous general exposition of the Buddha-dharma. △ Fourth, the Adornment.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely designated as 'adorning.'"
This passage cites the Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices to manifest non-abiding.

Regarding the manifestation of non-abiding through not dwelling in the six sense objects, the four fruits, or the Buddha-dharma, the Buddha further addresses this within the chapter on "Non-abiding Practice of Giving."
By means of the perfect, true wisdom of emptiness, one opens up the emptiness that gives rise to the small emptiness and small wisdom;

this is the locus where all dharmas are realized as the Mahāyāna. This principle is not only clarified repeatedly within these two chapters of the formal exposition, but even within the subsequent section on "Holding the Name and Hearing the Meaning," it is likewise stated that everything without exception converges and returns to non-abiding. △ Second, the conclusion and indication.
II. Generating the Mind. First, the direct instruction:
"Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should generate a pure mind in this way.
They should not generate a mind dwelling on forms; they should not generate a mind dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. They should generate [a mind] without dwelling anywhere."
Regarding that mind:
these two characters are words of conclusion. This is because the non-abiding nature-virtue is present before one;
thus, one must not cling to the four fruits of the Buddha-dharma or the adornments of the Tathāgata. Therefore, your initial question should have been: "How should one..."
"Abiding. I then answered you, saying: "All Bodhisattvas should not abide in such a way when generating the mind;

they should not abide in the six sense-objects or the myriad phenomena while generating the mind for the six perfections and the myriad practices. This statement directly presents the initial question and the initial answer, thereby concluding and clarifying the point.
"One should not abide in form to generate the mind" refers to what was stated above as "should not abide."
One should not dwell on form while giving rise to the mind of generosity, nor should one dwell on form while giving rise to the mind of the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-caryā*).
If there is even a single thing upon which one dwells, it is the defiled mind of the four marks of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).

When there is no dwelling whatsoever while giving rise to the mind of the ten thousand practices, then the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā* manifests before one; every single practice then arises in accordance with the nature (*dharmatā*). Therefore:
Although one gives rise to the mind throughout the entire day, that mind remains pure throughout the entire day.
Furthermore, "should not abide" means that the Vajra-jewel sword sweeps straight away the emotional defilements (*kleśa-rajas*) of the ten realms.

If followers of the Two Vehicles grasp this and take it to be the ultimate, they will sink into emptiness and dwell in stillness, becoming solitary and estranged from *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is further urged: "One should..."
"Generate the mind by dwelling nowhere. This has a specific reference;
it refers to the six perfections and myriad practices, such as the mind that welcomes guests and sees them off, or puts on clothes and eats food.

This is because putting on clothes and eating food, as well as the six perfections and myriad practices—each and every one of them—arise from the wondrous conduct of non-abiding *prajñā*. Therefore, every action is nothing other than *prajñā*.
That which is called "entering principle" (nyāya-praveśa) is termed "abiding," for by means of the dharma of non-abiding, one abides within the Prajñāpāramitā.
This refers to when Śākyamuni Buddha first conformed to human ways, carrying his alms bowl to beg for food.
I also find deep peace in this principle. Thus, as soon as Śūnyatāpāla had this single insight, he was struck with wonder at its rarity.
Furthermore, when the mind arises from non-abiding, it is not only the wholesome minds thus produced that constitute Prajñā;
even all unwholesome and neutral karmic retributions are likewise so. As the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra says: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established."

Regarding all phenomena (*sarvadharma*): in principle, they are the nature-virtues of the conditions and the understanding; in fact, they are the three causes of cultivated virtue. When deluded, they are the circulation of the three paths;
when awakened, they are the supreme functions within the fruit. These four layers are all established based upon the true reality (*tathatā*) within delusion.
If they were not identical to this nature, there would be no King Atyaṣṭi, the Brahmin Jotipāla, Devadatta, or Upāli.
"Su-mi-nü (Sumati), all are indeed evil dharmas. They arise from the non-abiding; thus, though they are evil, they are [inherently] nature.
If they arise through attachment, though they are good, they are likewise deviant. △ Second, the illustration by analogy.
"Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains. What do you think?
Would that body be large? Subhūti replied, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has said that what is not a body is called a 'large body'."
He then raises the concepts of "non-body" and "great body" as an analogy to clarify this, saying: "If one dwells in existence, even the king of mountains is small;
if one realizes non-body, even a mere hair-tip is great. If one wishes to examine the characteristics of phenomena in detail, one should rely on Master Youxi’s phrases:
"not dwelling yet arising, arising yet not dwelling," as well as the six stages of realization (*liù jí*) which clarify non-attainment.

The explanation of "abiding" and so forth. △ Third, the conclusion of the characteristics of giving to further manifest the two types of merit: nature-merit and form-merit. First, reiterating the merit of form as a basis for comparison:
"Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River; what do you think?"
"What do you think? Are all those grains of sand in the Ganges many? Subhūti replied, "Very many, World-Honored One.
Even the Ganges rivers alone are already countless; how much more so their sands? "Subhūti, I now tell you this in truth:
if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in those Ganges rivers..."
"If one were to give as a gift a thousand worlds, would one obtain much merit? Subhūti replied, "Very much, World-Honored One.
Regarding the fact that previously it was said only of giving a great trichiliocosm of jewels, while now it is said of giving as many great trichiliocosms of jewels as there are sands in the Ganges:
this merely cites the vastness of the physical objects given to further manifest the superior merit of upholding [the Dharma] without dwelling [on it]. There is no difference in quality between them.

This is a distinction. Even if one were to compare their respective acts of giving, there might still be some difference in degree; however, regarding the merit of their respective natures, there can certainly be no disparity between them.

Just as in the brief response given previously, where even a person of middling capacity who merely maintains [the precepts] attains superior blessings—comparable to a stupa or temple—how much more so for one who practices extensively, thereby becoming a person of the supreme Dharma, comparable to a sage or a holy one?
Thus, in contrast to what was stated in the previous brief answer, here it is shown that [the extensive practitioner] is without peer.

Regarding the "dwelling in the excellence of merit," it is said that space is inconceivable. Next, the initial "non-dwelling in the excellence of merit" is extensively explained as giving birth to the bodhi of all Buddhas.
This is sufficient to demonstrate the subtle wonder of the teaching’s harmonious integration and illuminating reflection.
How could there be any distinction between shallow and deep, or superior and inferior? △ Second, extensively revealing that the perfection of the nature constitutes the Buddha-dharma, in two parts:

First, briefly showing that the merit of the person who upholds it is supreme; second, [showing] the merit of the nature. As for why the merit of the nature must necessarily be explained in terms of extensive and brief upholding:
in the actual teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā, there are two gates—the extensive and the brief. Since the teachings are twofold, those who uphold them are likewise so.

Furthermore, within both the extensive and the concise [teachings], there must necessarily be self-maintenance and instruction of others; this is precisely the intent behind the entrustment of wealth in the *Prajñāpāramitā* so that it may be further transmitted.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Among these, however much should be taken and however much should be given; the concise is 'little,' while the extensive is 'much.'"
To practice it oneself is to take [the treasure]; to teach others is to give it. To receive, uphold, read, and recite it is the wealth entrusted by the Buddha;

to explain it for others is what the Buddha commands one to transmit and teach. Following this principle from beginning to end, there is nothing that does not apply in this way. Thus, a single person attains supreme merit.

The Buddha told Subhūti: "If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, from within this sutra, were to receive, uphold, and even recite as little as a four-line verse for the sake of others, the merit of this would surpass the former merit."
△ Second, the two places are like stūpas and shrines.
Furthermore, Subhūti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even if it be only a single four-line verse, you should know that this place should be honored by all the worlds—
devas, humans, and asuras— as if it were a stūpa or shrine of the Buddha.
△ Second, the superiority of merit for one who extensively upholds [the teaching] has two parts: first, the excellence of the person who accomplishes the supreme dharma;
second, the case of a person who is able to receive, uphold, read, and recite it in its entirety. Subhūti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, and rare dharma.
"Most supreme, foremost, and rare" is a laudatory epithet for the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
Therefore, when the question regarding its name arises later in the text, the Buddha answers directly with the full title of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*.
△ Second, the locations are like those of the sages and worthies.
Wherever this sutra is located, there is a Buddha, as well as his honored disciples. Those who have reached ultimate realization are Buddhas;
those who have attained partial realization are disciples. Regarding the three characters "ji," "wei," and "ruo":

they refer to the sages and worthies, yet they do not mean that [the place] is itself the sages and worthies. It is unnecessary to rely on the Wei translation’s inverted reading to explain them. △ Second, the entrustment.
The second [section] concerns the merit of hearing, upholding, and manifesting the names and meanings; it has two parts: first, the merit of upholding the name. First, the question:
At that time, Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, what should this sutra be named?
How should we uphold it?"

The preceding detailed and concise exposition on the principles of abiding, descending, and transcending has been fully concluded. It is now appropriate to inquire after the title so that it may be circulated.
What should this sutra be named? When Subhūti heard the meaning and intent of this sutra, he realized its transcendence and its inconceivable efficacy;
thus, there seemed to be no name by which it could be designated. How much more so regarding its upholding and recitation!
It is said: "One can thereby accomplish the most supreme and foremost rare Dharma. Thus, it is again impossible to designate a partial name to encompass such perfect virtue.
Therefore, it is asked: "By what name should this be called? △ Second, the answer has three parts: 1.
Explaining the name and teaching its upholding; 2. Direct instruction.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "This sūtra is named the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*. By this name, you should uphold it.
The Buddha explains that a "name" is that by which reality is summoned; since this sūtra possesses such qualities as being supreme, foremost, and most rare, [it is thus designated].

The actual substance of the three virtues must indeed be designated by using the full names of the three virtues, such as the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*, and not by means of a single character alone. △ Second, the double explanation.
Why is that? Subhūti, what the Buddha calls the perfection of wisdom is not the perfection of wisdom;
it is merely designated as the perfection of wisdom.
"Why is this so? [The text] below explains the meaning of the title, stating that among all six hundred fascicles of sutras, they are all called *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Why, then, is the specific term "Vajra" added here? Next, it explains the reason for adding the two characters "Vajra," saying:
"It is truly because this sword of Vajra-wisdom stands before one."
Not only does it sweep away and purify the attachments to the four marks (*catur-lakṣaṇa*) of the six realms of ordinary beings, but even the Dharma of Prajñā itself is not permitted to be clung to.
As it is said: "The great conflagration of Prajñā cannot be grasped from any side; to grasp it is to be burned.
If one becomes attached to Prajñā, it is likewise severed by the great function of the Vajra. Therefore, it is called Prajñāpāramitā.
"Honey" is not itself the Prajñāpāramitā; it is only through this negation that the signless Prajñāpāramitā is revealed.
These two characters, "is not" (ji fei), constitute the great function of the Vajra. This single response has fully exhausted the purport of adding the two characters "Vajra.
△ Second, the sequential revelation of non-abiding.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata has preached nothing. "Subhūti, what do you think?
Are all the atoms of dust contained within the trichiliocosm many? Subhūti said, "Very many, World-Honored One. "Subhūti, all..."
The Tathāgata speaks of atoms, yet they are not atoms; therefore they are called "atoms. The Tathāgata speaks of worlds, yet they are not worlds;
therefore they are called "worlds. Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks? "No, World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks. Why is that? The Tathāgata...
To speak of the thirty-two marks is to say they are non-marks; this is what is called the thirty-two marks.

Thus, the Tathāgata, by means of the supreme, non-abiding, wondrous wisdom, universally sweeps away all attachments to marks regarding the holy and the ordinary, thereby manifesting the victorious function of the Vajra.
He says: "It is not a world," "it is not a physical form," and "it is not preaching the Dharma. This refers to the upholding of the name.
This integrates all things and returns to the essential purport of the Mahāyāna school. △ Third, the conclusion indicating the merit:
"Subhūti, if there were good men or good women who, with as many bodies and lives as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, gave them as alms..."
If there were another person who, from this sutra, were to receive and uphold even as little as a four-line verse and explain it to others, their merit would be exceedingly great.
Now, one merely holds the name; why must the merit necessarily surpass that of giving away one's body and life? Yan said:
Its reputation is worth a thousand pieces of gold. Where the name exists, there the reality exists; it is like the title of the Most Honored One, which no minister can equal.
△ Second, the merit of hearing the meaning, in two parts: first, the formal explanation; second, hearing the meaning, in two parts.

I. Entrusting the departure from signs through the meaning of the sutra. II. Expanding the interpretation through emptiness. 1. Fortunate that the meaning has been understood, thereby clarifying the rarity of being able to hear it.
At that time, Subhūti, having heard this sutra being preached, deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and addressed the Buddha:
He said: "It is rare, World-Honored One! That the Buddha has preached such a profound sutra as this.

From my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this. World-Honored One, if there should be another person who hears this sutra and their faith becomes pure, they will immediately give rise to the mark of reality.
You should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit."
"Venerable One, this true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is itself the absence of marks. Therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name 'true mark.

This section first clarifies the meaning of the sūtra and subsequently clarifies its merit, culminating in the statement that 'the meaning of the sūtra is inconceivable, and its karmic fruit is likewise inconceivable,' which serves as a double conclusion.
For now, let us together, teacher and disciple, praise the meaning of the sūtra as we have heard it."
How rare! To hear this sutra being preached is indeed a matter of words. "Profoundly understanding the meaning and intent" refers to the significance elucidated beneath those words:

the great function of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* manifests before one, sweeping away all emotional attachments within the ten realms and returning to the true emptiness that is free from marks.
This is precisely what was clarified throughout the preceding sections as "neither this nor that. As for "intent," it is that which lies beyond the words.
The meaning revealed here is that true emptiness is not empty; each and every thing returns to the shore of the real mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
One realizes that all things are the Mahāyāna. This is precisely what was clarified in various preceding passages as being "named" [thus].
Therefore, he directly extols it, saying: "How rare! This "how rare" is different from the previous instance. The former was the first glimpse of the Tathāgata’s ordinary daily activities. Do not...
It is not that non-abiding *prajñā* has not manifested before one. It is like when one first beholds a celestial king’s jeweled palace and exclaims, "How rare!

Now, however, through winding questions and answers, the matter is explained in full detail and clarity. One deeply realizes that while emptiness is empty, it is not void; every dharma is entirely real.
It is as if one has already beheld Maitreya’s multi-storied pavilions, seeing them minutely—every five paces a pavilion, every ten paces another.
I have not had the leisure to speak exhaustively of all matters within the palace. Thus, what was previously glimpsed as vast is now seen in its entirety as subtle and profound;
hence it is called "rare. Nevertheless, the reason I again shed tears of sorrow is that since obtaining the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard such a sutra.
Were I to miss this even once, the loss would be even greater; therefore, I weep once more.
Shedding tears of compassion, he next sighed that among those who hear what is rare, they have now heard this sutra. Hearing it constitutes *śrutamayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of hearing);

believing and understanding it constitutes *cintāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of reflection); and upholding it constitutes *bhāvanāmayī-prajñā* (wisdom born of cultivation). Once these three wisdoms are complete, they shall likewise deeply understand the meaning and intent as I do today.
That the mind of faith is pure is the aforementioned meaning. Employing the great function of the vajra, one sweeps away all [delusions] into emptiness.
All things are utterly cut off, yet the essence of true emptiness is revealed. Not clinging to the emotional dust of the ten realms constitutes purity.
When the water of the sentient beings' minds is clear, the reflections of all Buddhas appear therein. True emptiness is not empty; it directly manifests the true mark (*dharmatā*).

It is like the metaphor of a spring pond where the inner water is clear and the jewel appears, or as clarity arises when a mirror is polished. While all phenomena do not arise, Prajñā arises—this is what is meant by "arising."
Regarding the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): one should know that the true mark has neither that which gives birth nor that which is born;

it merely reveals the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is metaphorically called "birth. This is what is meant by the so-called "eternal abiding for a thousand years and birth in a single morning.
This is the intended meaning of the previous explanation. Since all phenomena are empty, is this not the foremost *prajñā*? Since reality is born...
Observing these signs, one might ask: "Is this person not truly a rare individual who has already reached the further shore of the treasure-trove?
△ Second, praising the rarity of what is to be heard by reflecting on one's own past lack of understanding.
World-Honored One, for me to now hear such a sutra as this, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, would not be difficult.

However, if in a future age, during the final five hundred years, there should be sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, believe, understand, accept, and uphold it—such persons would be the most rare and extraordinary.
Why is this? Because such persons are without the mark of self, the mark of a person, or the mark of a sentient being.
It has no mark of a self. Why is this? The mark of a self is itself no-mark;
the marks of a person, a sentient being, and a life-span are themselves no-marks. For what reason? Because one who is free from all marks is called a Buddha.

I mean that we have already eliminated the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*) and have opened the way to enter the Mahāyāna; we are those at the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).
How much more so when we receive the Buddha’s earnest and skillful guidance, enabling us to open the treasury of our nature (*prakṛti-garbha*) and peer into the ultimate—this is not difficult.
However, during the final five hundred years, a time when those who are stubborn and difficult to transform prevail, when the sages and worthies have passed away, and the faculties of human beings...

Superficial and dull. If there are sentient beings who, upon hearing this sutra, are able to enter into both the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) and the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), and thus attain a semblance of seeing the nature (*dharmatā*), one should know that this semblance is itself the Buddha; it is the foremost rarity.
Next, the text explains the reason why it is the foremost rarity. The three characters "Why is this? (*kiṃ kāraṇam*) are words of inquiry. [The phrase] "the preceding part" refers to...
When faith is pure, one immediately gives rise to the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Having partially realized the secret treasury, such a person may indeed be called "foremost.

However, those who now merely believe, understand, and uphold [the teaching] are simply individuals at the stage of the five ranks (*pañca-varga*) or the six faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), still engaged in cultivation.
How can they also be called "foremost"? The text below explains this: One should know that because these people are already able to believe, understand, and uphold [the teaching], they have...
This refers to one who possesses both the wisdom of reflection and the wisdom of cultivation. From time to time, the great function of the vajra manifests before them;

they are forever free from the four marks and alone reveal the true emptiness. Therefore, at the stage of the purity of the six sense organs, the true path is able to penetrate, making it the foremost.
Why is this? To be free from all marks is precisely what is called being a Buddha; this explains the two rare and marvelous qualities.
[The word] "Why? (*katham*). In this context, for what reason are these three characters also interrogative terms? [The answer is:

It may be said that the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*) can be designated as the "first" because it is identical to the prior purity of faith (*śraddhā-viśuddhi*).

However, since such a person merely possesses cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-mayī-prajñā*) and has not yet attained the realization of the true reality (*dharmatā*), how can they be called "rare"? Therefore, he immediately explains it as follows:
I fear only that people’s minds are not empty. Since one can empty all that exists, this is precisely the emptiness of true emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

This non-emptiness is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). As it is said: "When the mirror is pure, clarity arises; when purity reaches its limit, light penetrates. If this were not the truth, what else could we wait for?
Therefore, this person is called one who has reached the shore of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), resembling the Buddhas; this is indeed rare.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the state free from all marks is precisely the meaning of the aforementioned profound understanding;

it is what is called the abode of the Buddhas, and it is the direction of the aforementioned profound realization. All of these clearly elucidate the essential principle of dwelling in the transcendence of marks. Now...
Śūnyatā-janman extracted the essential points from within the meaning of what he had heard; it was not that he spoke of other dharmas apart from the preceding text.
Since Śūnyatā-janman himself understood this dharma, he immediately used this very dharma to praise and model for future generations.
This is clearly evident in the text; let the students know this. II. The Tathāgata’s Confirmation, in two parts: A. Certification.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "So it is, so it is.

The double expression "so it is" is used because, although there are differences in the realization and cultivation of those who hear this sutra—such as Śūnyatā-janman (the one born of emptiness)—[they all attain the same result].
As for the fact that both equally attain the most rare and extraordinary merit, this is by no means erroneous or indiscriminate; therefore, both are affirmed.
△ Second, a profound exposition, which has two parts. First, describing the rarity of those who hear.
If, moreover, there should be someone who hears this sutra and is not startled, not terrified, and does not fear it, you should know that such a person is most rare.
This is a restatement of the preceding words of praise in their reverse order. [The Buddha] said: "Subhūti, what do you seek?"
It is because people possess such profound depth that [the Buddha] insists their faith must be pure so that the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa) may arise;
only after they have attained faith, understanding, and upholding [the teaching] does he grant them the status of being "most rare.

One must know that there are those who, upon hearing what the Tathāgata has spoken, employ vajra-like wisdom to sweep away all emotional attachments within the ten realms, thereby manifesting reality.
To be able to accept and understand this principle of rare wonder without being startled or terrified is precisely the initial mind of the five stages;

such a person is one who can accord with [the truth] in a single thought-moment. Therefore, even upon suddenly hearing that all things are empty and that the Buddha-dharma itself is empty, they are not startled.
Previously, they relied on the foremost Prajñā as the guide and the sovereign of the six pāramitās and myriad practices.
Now, it is likewise not departing, yet there is no fear. Previously, one relied upon Prajñā as a place of refuge; now, even though it departs into emptiness, there is no dread.
This is because one has already realized that within the substance of our own mind, prior to the state of non-delusion in original truth, there was no name or mark of "Prajñā.
Furthermore, after the ultimate fruit of realization, what guiding role could "Prajñā" possibly have?
Therefore, upon hearing this principle of true emptiness that sweeps away all marks, one is able to accept it with patience and without fear.
It should be known that such a person has already been able to perfectly subdue the five stages of dwelling (pañca-vihāra), and their contemplative practice (vipaśyanā) is equal to that of a Buddha.

As the "Chapter on Rejoicing" (*Anumodanā-parivarta*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* praises their inconceivable merit as being comparable to that of a Buddha, it says they are "most rare. This refers to the first [stage].
The character "Shen" (甚) signifies that the initial aspiration and the ultimate realization are non-different. Of these two states of mind, the former is difficult [to attain].

Since the Tathāgata has already deeply affirmed that even those at the stage of the five ranks of beginners who do not experience alarm or fear are themselves rare, this is difficult to believe according to principle;
therefore, he explains and clarifies it by addressing both phenomena and principle. △ Second, explaining through phenomena and principle in two parts. First:
According to the first principle.
Why is this? Subhūti, that which the Tathāgata calls the foremost pāramitā is not, in fact, a foremost pāramitā;
it is merely designated as the foremost pāramitā.
Why is this? The three characters [“Why? are interrogative terms. How could it be that this person is not startled or terrified—this is indeed marvelous!

The commentary states: Prajñā is the sovereign of the myriad practices and the six perfections. Now, as the great function of the Vajra stands before one, even the characteristics of the foremost Prajñā are not permitted to be clung to.
If one clings to Prajñā, it is identical to the four marks; therefore, it is swept away.

He set it aside and said: "This is not the foremost *pāramitā*. When ordinary people and those of the Lesser Vehicle hear such a teaching, there are none who do not feel startled, doubtful, or terrified.
Now, the person of the Perfect [Vehicle] has already deeply conformed to the true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) and the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*);
thus, they follow it with joy and are therefore neither startled nor afraid. Beneath true emptiness lies the eternally abiding true mark, wherein one can further dwell in peace."
Unshakable. This practitioner of contemplation is like a Buddha; because they share the same mind as a Buddha, it is said of them that this is "most rare.
△ Second, regarding the matter of patience, there are two parts. First, due to peaceful endurance, one is not startled or terrified.
Subhūti, the perfection of patience—what the Tathāgata calls the perfection of patience is not actually a perfection of patience;

it is designated as the "perfection of patience" because one hears this profound principle and is not startled. This is truly due to having already attained the two types of patience: the patience of suppression and the patience of compliance. Since patience has been perfected within oneself, [one is unshaken].

Unperturbed by favor or disgrace, at peace with both adversity and prosperity, they do not feel joy when honored by devas and nāgas, nor do they harbor anger or resentment when a wicked king cuts off their limbs.
Within the ten vehicles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, those who can practice such patient endurance are all non-retrogressive.
Now, hearing that both objects and wisdom are empty, those who lack patience will inevitably experience much alarm, doubt, and fear. Such a person...

Because one has already been able to fully perfect the patience of subduing [the afflictions], one is not startled or terrified. The *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The bodhisattva dwells on the ground of patience;
gentle, harmonious, and compliant, he is not abrupt or violent, and his mind is likewise not startled.
This single sentence explains that the perfection of patience results in being unstartled; it is a most rare and marvelous meaning. For a person of patience who still harbors even a trace of self...
To be "capable of endurance" while harboring the thought that one is capable of enduring insults is to fall into the four marks (*catur-nimitta*);

thus, one cannot attain the rare patience of the ultimate other shore. Now, this person dwells deeply at ease within the realm of insult; both self and other are forgotten, and the four marks are all swept away.
Therefore, it is said: "it is not. Once this state of "not being" is realized, each and every moment becomes the patience of ultimate reality.
Is this not indeed rare? △ Second, citing past events to explain that patience is free from marks.

Why is this so? Subhūti, when I was formerly cut and mangled in body by King Kali, at that time I had no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span. Why is this so? Because at that time...
In the past, when my limbs were severed joint by joint, if there had been any notion of a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span, I would have given rise to anger and resentment.
Subhūti, furthermore, I recall that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, I was a rishi of patience;
during all those lifetimes, there was no notion of a self, no notion of a person, no notion of a sentient being, and no notion of a life-span.
Why is this? Furthermore, these are words of inquiry. An objection is raised: "If a person can peacefully endure the ultimate truth, they will not be startled or terrified.
Now, if the Tathāgata further states that it is "not patience," then the one who possesses the capacity for endurance is likewise empty.
By what means of proof is it known that the one who practices patience is devoid of the marks of self and personhood? Thus, [the text] cites what the Tathāgata has already cultivated and...
To verify this through practice, one realizes that the cultivation of patience is entirely devoid of the four marks.
This is because while one may employ artifice during ordinary times, when faced with the great perils of birth and death, not even a hair’s breadth of contrivance will suffice. Therefore it is said:
"At that time, I was without the four marks. Why is this? He asks again: "How can Prajñā be without the four marks? Up to...
Regarding patience: because there is a sense of "I" who can endure, that which is endured becomes the object; thus this practice is established.

If this is so, what fault is there in there being four characteristics? Answer: If there were the characteristic of a self (*ātman*) or the characteristic of a person (*pudgala*), then it would not be the characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Why? [The three characters] are also an interrogative censure. How is it proven and known that when the Tathāgata practices patience, he has fully realized...?

"Is it that you lack the four marks? He then explained clearly: "When my body was being dismembered limb by limb, if even a slight sense of the 'four marks' such as the self had remained, anger and resentment would have arisen.
It is precisely because both personhood and selfhood were forgotten that anger and resentment did not arise."
The limbs and joints are restored. Because one practices patience while remaining detached from signs, one is at peace in both adverse and favorable circumstances.
One does not give rise to resentment toward unpleasant objects, nor does one give rise to attachment or joy toward pleasant objects; one does not experience alarm or fear upon hearing the profound.

Furthermore, because one is far removed from the four marks, it is said that this "patience" is not patience at all, but rather the manifestation of the true emptiness of *prajñā*. Dharma after dharma...
All of these are so. Therefore it is said: "This is called patience. It is the realization that true emptiness is not empty, reaching the further shore of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*).
Thus, it is granted that those who, from the very beginning, do not become startled or afraid are truly rare. Why is this chapter so extensive?
Because it is a point where the vital veins of the sutra are interconnected; every single word must find its proper place for the intent of the sutra to manifest.

△ Second, the summary and indication of the arising of the mind through detachment from signs (two parts). In the previous extensive explanation, first the non-abiding was sequentially revealed, and subsequently non-abiding was summarized to indicate the arising of the mind.
Now, within the meaning of the sūtra, first the detachment from signs is explained in detail, and subsequently the detachment from signs is summarized to indicate the arising of the mind.
As for why the locus of the arising of the mind is still called "non-abiding": [it is because...]
One must know that being free from marks is precisely non-abiding, and non-abiding is precisely being free from marks; these may be raised interchangeably to mutually reveal one another.
Thus, there is no mind arising from non-abiding.

The vessel-world is impermanent. When shattered into subtle dust, it is small and manifold; when joined together to form a world, it is large and one.
Yet, if it is within the Tathāgatagarbha, birth, death, largeness, and smallness cannot be found at all. Therefore, it is said that all things are "not so.
This "not so" is the manifestation of the essence of true emptiness. However, this true emptiness is not empty; each and every thing...
All are fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; therefore, they are all called "names.
These names are precisely the universal gateway of the *pāramitās*. As for the "unified totality" (*ekaghanasaṃjñā*), it is that which is ineffable.
Yet, ordinary people greedily cling to these phenomena. Although this unified totality is but a false name and an illusory appearance, it does not exist apart from [the nature of reality].
The Dharma-realm is, from the very outset, an inconceivable realm that transcends names and verbal expression;
therefore, it is said to be the ineffable true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). If so, why does the Tathāgata not explain it?

If the Tathāgata were to employ even a single word of explanation, I fear that ordinary people, failing to understand what is taught, would immediately give rise to craving and attachment toward those things.
[The Buddha] said, "Subhūti, it is because views arise in accordance with words that they cannot be spoken of. △ Third, the equality of all views that have been taught:
Subhūti, if someone were to say, 'The Buddha has taught the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span,' Subhūti, what do you think?
Would this person understand the meaning of what I have taught? "No, World-Honored One. This person would not."

I understand the meaning of what the Tathāgata has taught. Why is this? World-Honored One, although the four views—the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span—are the most extreme states of delusion for sentient beings, they do not leave so much as a hair’s breadth of residue upon the essence of true emptiness.
Because they are delusions, all are "not" [the reality]. However, the *āśraya-parāvṛtti* (transformation of the basis) occurs entirely within one’s own most excellent mind.
If even the form and mind of the hells are ultimately [transformed], how much more so these various views—could they not be the equal, true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*)? Therefore it is said:

"These are called the view of self, the view of person," and so forth. One must know that whenever the term "is called" (*saṃjñaka*) is used throughout the preceding and following sections, it refers to the *pāramitā*.

Therefore, when Śūnyatājanman arrived, he had already attained a profound understanding of the true reality of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-dharmatā*) and clearly realized that all phenomena are the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).

Thus, his realization was revealed as such—penetrating, liberated, perfect, and pure. The Buddha, based on his perfect understanding, then fully revealed and instructed him so that he might enter into the ultimate truth.

One must, with respect to the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, and the eighty thousand dharmas of arising and ceasing, understand and believe in each and every one as being the true reality of ultimate emptiness.
Furthermore, their phenomenal characteristics (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) must all be brought into accord with this. Only in this way is one truly able to take possession of and know the treasury.

△ Third Major Section: Circulation, in two parts. First, the exhortation to circulate; second, the enumeration of benefits to encourage circulation.

Subhūti, if there were someone who took seven treasures filling immeasurable asaṃkhyeya worlds and used them for giving as alms, and if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who has resolved upon bodhicitta and upholds this sutra—even [a small portion thereof]—[the latter would generate greater merit].
To receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain even four lines of verse from this [sūtra] for others, one’s merit will surpass that of the former;
this should be understood. △ Second, showing the method for circulation.
How does one expound the Dharma for others? Without grasping at signs, remaining as suchness, unshakable. Why is this?
All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, and a shadow; they are like dew and like lightning. One should contemplate them in this way.

Since the essential purport of the True Dharma Sūtras all converge upon the gate of the Mahāyāna’s true mark (*dharmatā*), where the object is suchness and wisdom is suchness, and wisdom is suchness and the object is suchness, those who later propagate this sūtra should likewise abide correctly according to the sūtra:
remaining unmoved by the conditioned and not grasping at any signs. Only then can one act as one speaks and speak as one acts. Thus it should be done.
When a person delivers a discourse, one must know that movement is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), and the conditioned is movement.
To grasp at signs is not to accord with suchness (*tathatā*); suchness is precisely the non-grasping of signs. Below, the text interrogates why there must be neither movement nor grasping.

Why is this? The three characters [“why,” “because,” and “therefore”] are interrogative terms. Question: For what reason must one who expounds the Dharma for others be without grasping and without movement?
Answer: It is because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are like dreams and illusions and lack substantial reality.
Those who propagate the *Prajñāpāramitā* and uphold the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of the Vaipulya teachings should contemplate them in this manner.
One should not, on the contrary, give rise to grasping or attachment. △ Second, the conclusion of the benefits and the circulation [of the text]:
After the Buddha had spoken this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, as well as the bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, [and upāsikās...]
Upāsikā. Having heard what the Buddha had spoken, all those in the world—gods, humans, and asuras—were filled with great joy;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
This concludes the Essential Meaning of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
